newsitem.title: GERMANY: Weak Ifo data bolsters German rate cut hopes.
newsitem.headline: Weak Ifo data bolsters German rate cut hopes.

text.p: A sharper-than-expected fall in a key barometer of business climate lent weight to worries about the strength of the German economy on Tuesday while prompting renewed hope for a further cut in interest rates.

A Reuter poll of 10 economists on forecasts for Bundesbank interest rates in 1997 showed that six expected a further cut in rates in this economic cycle, a big change from just one in a similar poll two weeks ago.

The poll was conducted just a few hours after the Munich-based IFO institute said the west German climate index -- the most closely-watched of its three main confidence barometers -- fell to 95.8 in December from November's 96.9.
The business conditions and business expectations measures also dropped -- to 89.8 and 101.8, respectively. In November the conditions index stood at 91.4 and expectations at 102.4.
For east Germany, the business climate measure dropped to 104.4 from 104.8 in November.
Economists said the worse than expected data provided yet more evidence that the German recovery was on rocky ground.

Excerpts from a draft official report on the German economy obtained by Reuters on Tuesday evening showed the government was sticking with a forecast for a sharp rise in growth to 2.5 percent this year, up from 1.4 percent in 1996.

But other key forecasts from the report -- due for release next week -- were less positive. The unemployment rate was pencilled in at a high 11 percent, while growth in industrial investment was seen growing by just 1.5 percent.
The report showed Bonn was sticking to the growth forecast underpinning Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bid to cut state borrowing and qualify for European monetary union.
Waigel's austerity aims, combined with intense concern about the recent record jobless figures, are seen stepping up pressure on the Bundesbank to lower interest rates.
"Pressure on the Bundesbank is increasing, also since the government finds itself in a strait-jacket," Stefan Schneider at Banque Paribas Capital Management in Frankfurt said.

However, all but one economist polled said that the Bundesbank was likely to hold off for at least several weeks before making a further move, even though inflation was now expected to remain below two percent in the long term.
Bundesbank council member Helmut Hesse made clear in a speech late on Tuesday that he believed there was no need to change interest rates any time soon.
Speaking in the eastern German town of Magdeburg, Hesse noted that long-term rates were already low and that this was a critical factor for German economic growth.
"Under the given conditions it is probably not possible for the Bundesbank to steer long-term rates lower," he said.

Economists generally pinpointed the recent sharp rise in the dollar to above 1.60 marks and a sharp slide in bond market interest rates to around 5.75 percent as the two most important factors blocking a rate move -- at least for now.

"The Bundesbank doesn't want to give any false impressions to the currency markets. The mark is in meltdown at the moment and they don't want to be seen endorsing a weaker mark," said David Brown at Bear Stearns.

Although the recent depreciation of the mark is a boon for the economy as it helps exports, an excessively large fall could destabilise it through imported inflation, which would also be at odds with the Bundesbank's stability aims.

Schneider at Paribas warned of the possible negative effect on the bond market of an unexpected cut. Low long-term interest rates are positive for the economy as most corporate borrowing is linked to long-term rates.
"The Bundesbank won't move soon. Bund yields could fall further in the short term. I believe 5.50 percent is possible," Schneider said.

But almost half of the economists polled stuck with their view that the Lombard and discount rates had already bottomed with the discount already at a record low of 2.50 percent and the Lombard rate, at 4.50 percent, also near its lows.
